# **Chapter II. The Industry, the Company, and Its Product or Service**

---

## **A. The Industry**

### **A.1 Industry Definition**

Hakbang belongs to the online recruitment and HR technology industry. This industry covers digital platforms and software that help employers find, screen, and hire workers, and help job seekers find work. Because Hakbang matches job seekers to training that leads to a job, it also overlaps with the workforce development and enterprise-based training industry, where companies train people for roles in their own organizations. Its first employer market is the information technology and business process management (IT-BPM) industry, one of the largest sources of formal entry-level jobs in the Philippines.

| Industry Level | Industry |
| :---- | :---- |
| Primary | Online recruitment and HR technology (job matching platforms, talent marketplaces) |
| Secondary | Workforce development and enterprise-based training (train-to-hire, upskilling) |
| Employer market served | IT-BPM (contact centers, back office, technical support, global capability centers) |

*Table 2.1. Industry Classification of Hakbang*

### **A.2 Industry Size**

The Philippine human resource (HR) technology market reached USD 774.3 million in 2025\. This market includes recruitment platforms like Hakbang, along with payroll, HR management, and training software.

The employer market Hakbang serves is much larger. The Philippine IT-BPM industry is poised to reach about \$42 billion in export revenues and nearly 1.97 million jobs in 2026\. With close to 2 million workers and steady hiring of entry-level staff, IT-BPM is a large and stable source of demand for Hakbang's partner employers.

### **A.3 Growth Rate**

The Philippine HR technology market is projected to reach USD 1,452.3 million by 2034, a growth rate (CAGR) of 7.24% during 2026-2034. Rising online recruitment is a major factor fueling this growth, as more employers and job seekers rely on digital platforms for faster, more efficient hiring.

Online hiring activity is also rising. Online hiring in the Philippines strengthened in March 2026, with the foundit Insights Tracker rising 16% year-on-year, and hiring grew by 12% over the past six months, supported by economic expansion and growing demand for logistics, digital, and healthcare talent. In IT-BPM, the industry grew faster than the global market despite macroeconomic headwinds, according to IBPAP.

### **A.4 Trends Shaping the Industry**

The industry is being shaped by four main trends.

1. **The shift to online hiring.** Job seekers, especially fresh graduates, now look for work mainly through phone apps, job boards, LinkedIn, and Facebook groups. Employers are moving their hiring to digital channels as well.  
2. **Skills-based hiring.** Employers are starting to judge applicants more by their skills and less by their degrees or past job titles. This helps fresh graduates who lack experience but can show the skills a role needs, and it fits Hakbang’s use of skills in the Living Profile.  
3. **Upskilling as an industry priority.** IBPAP's priorities for 2026 are scaling AI responsibly, expanding global capability centers, and accelerating upskilling. More employers now see training as part of hiring, which matches Hakbang's train-to-hire model.  
4. **Government support for company-led training.** New laws encourage companies to train workers themselves (see Government Regulations below).

### **A.5 Emerging Technologies**

**Artificial intelligence (AI)** is the main technology changing both the jobs and the way people are hired for them. In IT-BPM, 67 percent of IBPAP member firms have incorporated AI tools into their operations. The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas expects generative AI to augment rather than displace jobs in the near term, but stresses the urgent need for workforce reskilling and upskilling.

In recruitment, AI is used to screen resumes, match candidates to jobs, and assess skills. In the United States, 25.9% of employers reported using AI in hiring, up from 14.7% in 2024\. Employers want job boards to go beyond postings and include prescreening, skills assessments, and talent pipelining.

| Technology | How Hakbang Uses It |
| :---- | :---- |
| Matching algorithms | Pair each job seeker's Living Profile with the training tracks that fit them best |
| AI skill-gap detection | Shows job seekers what they still need to learn for each track |
| Digital two-sided platform | Connects job seekers and verified employers in one place, with progress tracking |

*Table 2.2. Emerging Technologies and How Hakbang Uses Them*

### **A.6 Government Regulations**

Several Philippine laws affect how Hakbang operates.

| Law or Rule | What It Means for Hakbang |
| :---- | :---- |
| Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10173\) | Hakbang collects personal data in each Living Profile, so it must get consent, protect the data, and share it only with employers the job seeker applies to. |
| Enterprise-Based Education and Training (EBET) Framework Act (Republic Act No. 12063\) | Signed in November 2024, the law expands enterprise-based training, strengthens industry participation in curriculum development, and enhances on-the-job training and apprenticeship programs (Manila Bulletin, 2025). It also enhances tax incentives for participating enterprises and recognizes IT-BPM among the key sectors for industry-designed training programs (TESDA, 2025). This gives partner companies more reason to run train-to-hire programs. |
| Labor Code of the Philippines and DOLE rules on recruitment and placement | Private recruitment for local employment is regulated by the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE). Hakbang will confirm with DOLE whether its matching service requires a license. Partner employers must also hire trainees under formal employment contracts with mandatory benefits (SSS, PhilHealth, and Pag-IBIG). |
| Public Employment Service Office (PESO) Act (Republic Act No. 8759\) | This law sets up PESOs in local government units, which Hakbang plans to work with as channel partners. |

*Table 2.3. Philippine Laws and Regulations Affecting Hakbang*

### **A.7 Industry Challenges**

| Challenge | Description |
| :---- | :---- |
| Skill mismatch | Employers report many applicants but few who are qualified. The IT-BPM industry spends about P1.4 billion a year on talent development, yet still lists the supply of employable talent among its main challenges for 2026 (Manila Times, 2026; Philstar, 2026a). |
| Limited company training | Only 28.6% of establishments with 10 or more workers gave job-related training in 2023 (Philippine Statistics Authority \[PSA\], n.d.). Most workers have to find and pay for training on their own. |
| Underemployment among young workers | In March 2026, underemployment was 12.3%, and about 753,000 of 5.76 million employed youth were underemployed (PSA, 2026). |
| Fake job posts and unfair training setups | Scam postings and unpaid "free training" with no job at the end are common, which makes job seekers distrust online platforms. |
| AI-driven change in jobs | As AI takes over routine tasks, entry-level roles are changing faster than public training can keep up. Government-funded AI training programs projected for 2026 may cover about 68,000 learners, a small portion of the 1.9 million-strong IT-BPM workforce (Philstar, 2026b). |
| Data privacy and AI risks | For firms adopting AI, implementation costs, system integration, and data privacy concerns are key hurdles (Bengzon, 2024). A matching platform must also avoid unfair bias, such as ranking applicants lower because of the school they attended. |

*Table 2.4. Industry Challenges Facing Train-to-Hire Platforms*

*Table 2.5. PESTLE Analysis of the Train-to-Hire Industry*

The PESTLE results point one way. Government policy, employer demand, and job seeker behavior all favor a trusted train-to-hire channel. The two factors we must manage are legal compliance (data privacy and the DOLE license question) and the effect of AI on entry-level jobs.

#### ***A.8.2 Porter's Five Forces***

***![][image2]***

*Figure 2.1. Porter's Five Forces for the Philippine Train-to-Hire Market*

| Force | Level | Reason | Our response |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Threat of new entrants | Medium | Cloud tools make a job app cheap to build. Trust, a verified employer network, and two-sided scale take years to build, and NPC and DOLE rules add steps. | Sign employers first and build a hire and retention record early (Ch. II, D.1). |
| Bargaining power of buyers (employers) | High | Employers can post for free on Jobstreet Lite for up to 30 days (Jobstreet, n.d.-a) and on PhilJobNet at no cost (PhilJobNet, n.d.). Large BPOs run in-house academies. | Charge only on hire, offer a half-price pilot, and prove a lower cost per hire with data (Ch. IV, B and C). |
| Bargaining power of suppliers | Medium | Partner employers supply the training content and the jobs, so they act as both supplier and buyer. Cloud and AI vendors have substitutes, but switching takes effort. Job seekers are plentiful as individuals. | Keep our own data and matching logic, export backups monthly, and use standard tools that more than one vendor supports (Ch. VI, D). |
| Threat of substitutes | High | Job boards, Facebook groups, referrals, agencies, TESDA Online, and in-house training all solve part of the problem. | Win on the full path from match to signed contract, which no substitute offers in one place. |
| Rivalry among competitors | Medium | Jobstreet, LinkedIn, and Kalibrr compete hard for employer budgets. None of them offers company-sponsored training with a hiring commitment, so rivalry inside the train-to-hire niche is still low. | Stay focused on the niche and grow the network before incumbents add training features. |

*Table 2.6. Porter's Five Forces Analysis*

Two forces are high: employer bargaining power and substitutes. Both come from the many free or cheap ways employers already reach applicants. Hakbang cannot beat these options on price alone, so it competes on outcomes: trained, pre-matched hires and a fee that employers pay only after a hire. Rivalry in our niche is still moderate, which gives a new entrant a window to build its network before larger players respond.

## **B. The Company and the Concept**

### **B.1 Company Background**

Team Unlad is a group of five students who came together to build a venture around a problem they know firsthand. "Unlad" is the Filipino word for progress or growth, and the team chose it because it describes what its members want for themselves and for others like them: a real chance to move forward in their careers.

The members of Team Unlad are soon-to-be graduates with no formal work experience, and are searching for jobs themselves. Like many young Filipinos, they believed a diploma would be enough to open doors. They soon found that most entry-level job posts still ask for one to two years of experience. That leaves new graduates caught in a familiar cycle: they cannot get hired without experience, and they cannot get experience without being hired.

The search also brought problems beyond the rejections. The members sent out applications that were never answered, and they came across job posts that turned out to be fake or misleading. Some were offered "free training" that ended with no job offer. Others saw batchmates take jobs unrelated to their courses, or part-time work with no benefits to earn something while they kept searching. The members also learned that employers want job-ready workers but seldom have a clear way to find and train fresh graduates who are willing to learn. Each failed application was frustrating, and it was also a sign that the system connecting graduates to employers was not working well for either side.

These shared experiences led Team Unlad to pursue Hakbang. The team asked a simple question: what if training led straight to a job, and graduates could trust that the company training them intended to hire them? Hakbang is the team's answer. Because the founders are part of the market they want to serve, they understand its fears and needs. They know which channels graduates use, and they can reach them through batchmates, student organizations, and school networks.

### **B.2 Mission**

To connect Filipino job seekers with verified employers that train and hire them, so that every completed training leads to a real, formal job.

### **B.3 Vision**

To become the most trusted train-to-hire platform in the Philippines, helping move workers from unemployment, underemployment, and informal work into decent jobs.

### **B.4 Core Values**

* **Trust:** Only verified companies with real train-to-hire programs are listed.  
* **Transparency:** Every step, from match to hiring, is visible to the job seeker.  
* **Growth:** Each trainee leaves with new skills and verified endorsements, whether or not they are hired.

### **B.5 Business Concept**

Hakbang is a digital platform that connects job seekers only with verified companies that offer train-to-hire programs. Hakbang does not create training content. Partner companies provide the training, and Hakbang acts as the marketplace, matcher, and progress tracker. A simple way to describe it is "Grab for train-to-hire": just as Grab matches a passenger with a nearby driver, Hakbang matches a job seeker with a company that will train and hire them.

Hakbang is a two-sided market. Job seekers are the end users and use the platform for free. Employers are the paying customers and pay a success fee only when a trainee is hired under a formal employment contract. Graduates need a first job and proof of skills, while employers are willing to train but struggle to find the right people to train.

### **B.6 Business Model**

Figure 2.2 puts it into a Business Model Canvas (Osterwalder & Pigneur, 2010). The canvas shows both sides of the market: job seekers who use Hakbang for free and employers who pay per hire.

![][image3]

*Figure 2.2. Hakbang Business Model Canvas*

| Block | Hakbang |
| :---- | :---- |
| Customer segments | Users: fresh college graduates in Metro Manila, 0 to 2 years out of school, who are jobless or mismatched. Payers: talent acquisition, HR, and L\&D leads at mid-size BPO and IT-BPM firms. |
| Value propositions | Job seekers: a free, verified path from training to a formal job, with endorsements that stay on the profile. Employers: pre-matched, motivated trainees, and a fee only when a trainee is hired. |
| Channels | Web app (PWA) in Year 1, a mobile app from Year 2 if Year 1 targets are met, employer dashboard, direct sales, university career offices, student organizations, Facebook and TikTok, batchmate referrals.  |
| Customer relationships | Self-service app with in-app chat for job seekers. One named contact, a monthly hiring report, and a replacement guarantee for employers. |
| Revenue streams | Success fee of P5,000 per hire (P2,500 pilot rate, P4,000 volume rate). Employer Pro dashboard at P10,000 a month from Year 2\. Featured listings later. |

| Key activities | Employer verification, platform development, track onboarding, matching, progress tracking, employer sales, and community marketing. |
| Key partners | BPO and IT-BPM firms and GCCs, university career offices, LGU PESOs, TESDA and IBPAP (later), and cloud and AI providers. |

*Table 2.7. Business Model Canvas Explained*

Hakbang runs a two-sided platform model. Employers fund the platform, job seekers create the supply of trainees, and each successful hire produces revenue. The model is asset-light: partner companies build the training, so Hakbang spends its money on software, verification, and sales.

### **B.7 Business Processes**

Hakbang runs three core processes. Each diagram shows who does each step. Light green boxes are job seeker steps, dark green boxes are Hakbang steps, and beige boxes are employer steps.

#### ***Process 1: Employer Onboarding and Verification***

***![][image4]***

*Figure 2.3. Employer Onboarding and Verification Process*

1. The employer creates an account on the employer dashboard.  
2. The employer uploads its SEC or DTI registration, BIR Certificate of Registration (Form 2303), and business permit, the same documents PhilJobNet requires (PhilJobNet, n.d.).  
3. The Hakbang team checks the documents against a verification checklist. If something is missing, we ask for it. If the employer fails the check, we reject the account.  
4. A verified employer signs the partner agreement, which lists the track, slots, hiring commitment, fee, and data rules.  
5. The employer posts a track with modules, schedule, allowance, and hiring criteria.  
6. We review the track terms. The track goes live with a "Verified Employer" badge.

#### ***Process 2: Job Seeker Train-to-Hire Journey***

***![][image5]***

*Figure 2.4. Job Seeker Train-to-Hire Process from v1.5*

1. The job seeker signs up, gives consent under the Data Privacy Act, and uploads a resume.  
2. The AI fills in the Living Profile, and the job seeker checks and edits it.  
3. Smart Matching ranks tracks by skills, location, and schedule. The AI Skill-Gap Check shows what to prepare.  
4. The job seeker applies, and the employer reviews the shortlist and accepts trainees.  
5. The trainee completes the modules. The Progress Tracker shows results and deadlines, and the employer adds an endorsement after each module.  
6. If the trainee passes the final assessment, the employer offers a formal contract. If not, the endorsements stay on the profile and Smart Matching suggests the next track.

#### ***Process 3: Hiring, Billing, and Guarantee***

***![][image6]***

*Figure 2.5. Hiring, Billing, and Replacement Guarantee Process*

1. The employer confirms the hire in the dashboard, and the trainee signs the employment contract.  
2. Hakbang records the hire and adds it to the month's invoice.  
3. At month end, we bill the employer for all hires made that month, with 30-day payment terms.  
4. We follow each hire for 90 days. If a hire leaves early, the employer gets a free replacement from the next batch, or a 50% credit if no fit comes up within 60 days.  
5. Each month, the employer receives a hiring report with cost per hire and retention.

Hakbang starts as a mobile-first web app with two sides: a web app that job seekers open in any phone browser, and a dashboard for employers. A dedicated mobile app follows in Year 2 only if we reach our Year 1 targets (Ch. II, D.3).

### **C.1 Features**

| Feature | User | What It Does |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Living Profile | Job seeker | Stores skills, school, course, location, preferences, and resume. It updates automatically as the user completes training and earns endorsements. |
| Smart Matching | Both | Pairs job seekers with company-sponsored training tracks based on fit, location, and schedule. |
| AI Skill-Gap Check | Job seeker | Shows which skills a user is missing for a track and suggests what to prepare before applying. |
| Train-to-Hire Tracks | Both | Company-designed training (readings, online tests, or face-to-face sessions) with clear terms: length, allowance if any, and hiring criteria. |
| Progress Tracker | Both | Shows each step from match to hiring, including test results and deadlines. |
| Verified Endorsements | Job seeker | Employers add endorsements to the profile after each completed module. These stay on the profile even if the trainee is not hired. |
| Employer Verification | Job seeker | Checks business registration and program legitimacy before a company can post a track. |
| Employer Dashboard | Employer | Lets talent and training leads post tracks, review matched candidates, monitor progress, and confirm hires. |

*Table 2.8. Hakbang Platform Features*

Figure 2.7 shows how the parts of the technology stack connect. Job seekers, employers, and the Hakbang team reach the Next.js app on Vercel over HTTPS. They also call outside services for AI features and notifications, and the app sends usage data to Google Analytics. ### **C.4 Use Cases**

**Use Case 1: Fresh graduate who keeps getting rejected for "no experience"**

Paolo is a BSBA graduate who has been job hunting for eight months while working part-time at a mall.

1. He signs up and builds his Living Profile by uploading his resume. The AI reads it and fills in his skills, course, and school, which he checks and edits.  
2. Smart Matching shows him three train-to-hire tracks from verified BPOs, ranked by fit, location, and schedule. He picks a back-office track in Ortigas with weekend sessions he can attend around his mall shifts.  
3. The AI Skill-Gap Check shows he is missing basic spreadsheet skills, so he reviews them before the track starts.  
4. He completes the company's online modules and a face-to-face assessment. The Progress Tracker shows his test results and deadlines, and he earns a Verified Endorsement after each module.  
5. He passes and is hired under a formal contract with SSS, PhilHealth, and Pag-IBIG benefits.

**Pain solved:** Paolo no longer competes on experience he does not have. He gets in by completing training the employer designed.

**Use Case 2: Graduate who was burned by a "free training" with no job offer**

Bea finished a company's free training last year, but no job offer came. She no longer trusts online postings.

1. She sees that every company on Hakbang has passed Employer Verification.  
2. Each track she views states its length, any allowance, and the hiring criteria before she applies.  
3. She joins a track and tracks her standing at every step. She knows what she needs to score to be hired.  
4. If she is not hired, her Verified Endorsements stay on her profile. Other employers can see them, and Smart Matching uses them to suggest her next track.

**Pain solved:** Bea knows the company is real, the terms are clear, and her effort counts even if one track does not end in a hire.

**Use Case 3: Graduating student preparing for the job market**

Marco is a fourth-year IT student who will graduate in four months.

1. He creates his Living Profile early and runs the AI Skill-Gap Check on junior IT support tracks.  
2. He uses his last semester to build the missing skills, such as basic networking.  
3. Once he graduates, he is matched to a track that starts within weeks, without a long job search.

**Pain solved:** Marco shortens the gap between graduation and his first job.

**Use Case 4: BPO training lead who needs to fill seats every month**

Carla is the talent acquisition and training lead at a mid-size BPO and must fill 40 to 60 entry-level seats a month.

1. She posts a customer service track on the Employer Dashboard, with training modules, schedule, and hiring criteria.  
2. Smart Matching sends her a shortlist of candidates who fit the role, location, and schedule, instead of hundreds of unscreened applications.  
3. She monitors each trainee's test results and completion in one dashboard and adds endorsements as they finish modules.  
4. She confirms the hires in the dashboard. Hakbang charges the success fee only for trainees who are hired.

**Pain solved:** Carla spends less time screening, loses less training budget to dropouts, and pays only for results.

**Use Case 5: University career office or LGU PESO as a channel partner**

A university career services office wants to improve its graduates' placement rate.

1. The office promotes Hakbang to graduating students and alumni through its pages and on-campus sessions.  
2. Students sign up and get matched to verified train-to-hire tracks.  
3. The office receives summary data on how many of its graduates were matched, trained, and hired. Hakbang shares only aggregate data, not personal profiles, in line with the Data Privacy Act.

**Pain solved:** The partner gets a reliable placement channel and data it can report, at no cost.

### **C.5 Customer Value Proposition**

**For job seekers:** "A verified path from training to a real job, so you take the next step (hakbang) with a job offer at the end."

**For employers:** "Pre-matched, motivated trainees, and you pay only when a trainee is hired."

The table below links each feature to its benefit and the value it creates, following the Feature → Benefit → Value framework.

| Feature | Benefit | Value |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Living Profile | Job seekers build one profile that grows with each training they finish | Less time filling out applications and a stronger record over time |
| Smart Matching | Job seekers see only tracks that fit them; employers see only candidates who fit | Shorter job search for job seekers; less screening work for employers |
| AI Skill-Gap Check | Job seekers know what to learn before applying | Higher chance of passing training and getting hired |
| Train-to-Hire Tracks | Training leads directly to a job, with terms stated up front | A clear path from training to formal employment |
| Progress Tracker | Both sides see where each trainee stands at every step | Less uncertainty for job seekers; easier planning for employers |
| Verified Endorsements | Completed training is recorded by the employer and stays on the profile | Proof of skills that helps job seekers even if they are not hired by one company |
| Employer Verification | Only legitimate companies can post tracks | Protection from scams and unpaid training with no job |
| Employer Dashboard | Training leads manage tracks, candidates, and hires in one place | Faster hiring and lower cost per hire |
| Success-fee pricing | Employers pay only when a trainee is hired; job seekers pay nothing | Lower risk for employers and no cost barrier for job seekers |

*Table 2.11. Feature, Benefit, and Value Framework*

## **D. Entry and Growth Strategy**

Hakbang will enter the market through one narrow, reachable segment, prove that train-to-hire works there, and then expand to nearby segments and regions using the same platform.

### **D.1 Market Entry Strategy**

Hakbang's beachhead market is **fresh college graduates (0 to 2 years after graduation) in Metro Manila who are jobless or working in jobs unrelated to their course**, matched with **entry-level IT-BPM roles** such as customer service, technical support, back office, and junior data and IT roles.

We chose this segment because it scored highest (24 out of 25\) in our segmentation matrix:

* **Easy to reach.** As college students, the team can reach fresh graduates through batchmates, university career offices, org pages, and graduate Facebook groups.  
* **Strong employer demand.** IT-BPM firms already train their new hires, so the train-to-hire model is familiar to them.  
* **Fully digital.** Fresh graduates already job-hunt on their phones and can use the app with little help.  
* **Word of mouth.** Graduates in the same batch talk to each other, so one successful hire spreads quickly.

Because Hakbang is a two-sided platform, the order of entry matters. **Employers come first.** We will sign partner companies before opening the app to job seekers, so the first users find real training tracks waiting for them instead of an empty platform.

### **D.2 Customer Acquisition**

| Customer | How we acquire them | Who leads it |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Partner employers (BPO and IT-BPM firms, GCCs) | Direct outreach to talent acquisition, HR, and L\&D leads through LinkedIn, alumni networks, and referrals; customer interviews that turn into sales conversations; a no-risk pilot offer | CEO, with the COO and CFO |
| Job seekers (fresh graduates) | University career offices and org pages, graduate Facebook groups and Discord or Messenger communities, on-campus info sessions, and batchmate referrals | CMO, with the COO |
| Channel partners (universities and LGU PESOs) | Meetings with career services offices and PESO officers, starting with the partners in our interview list | CEO and COO |

*Table 2.12. Customer Acquisition Channels and Owners*

### **D.3 Launch Strategy**

The launch happens in three phases.

| Phase | Main activities | Goal to move to the next phase |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Phase 1: Validate | Interview 20 respondents (12 job seekers, 6 employers, 2 ecosystem partners); test the success fee and employer willingness to pay; refine the personas and pricing | Interview results confirm the main pain points and at least a few employers agree to a pilot |
| Phase 2: Build the MVP | Build the Living Profile, rules-based matching, progress tracker, and employer dashboard; set up the employer verification process | A working app that pilot employers and job seekers can use |
| Phase 3: Launch | Open the platform to job seekers from partner universities and graduate communities in Metro Manila; promote it through social media, campus sessions, and referrals | Signed employer partners, an active base of job seekers, and the first hires |

*Table 2.13. Launch Phases and Transition Goals*

### **D.4 Pilot Deployment**

Before a full launch, Hakbang will run a pilot cohort with a small number of partner employers.

* **Partners:** A small number of mid-size BPO or IT-BPM firms in Metro Manila, each running one train-to-hire track.  
* **Participants:** A small cohort of fresh graduates recruited through one or two partner universities and graduate Facebook groups.  
* **Offer to employers:** No upfront cost. The success fee is charged only for trainees who are hired.  
* **What we measure:**  
  * Number of trainees matched and the training completion rate  
  * Hire rate (trainees who pass and are hired)  
  * Three-month retention of hires  
  * Time saved by employers in screening  
  * Feedback from both sides on the app  
* **What we do with the results:** Fix problems in matching and the app, adjust the success fee, and use the hire rate and retention results as proof when signing more employers.

### **D.5 Strategic Partnerships**

| Partner | What they give Hakbang | What they get |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| BPO and IT-BPM firms, GCCs | Training tracks and job openings; success-fee revenue | Pre-matched trainees and lower cost per hire |
| University career services offices | Access to graduating students and alumni; credibility with students | A placement channel and summary placement data for their reports |
| LGU Public Employment Service Offices (PESOs) | Access to job seekers in their cities; job fair data; later, access to underemployed and informal workers | A digital tool that connects their job seekers to verified employers |
| TESDA and TESDA-accredited training centers (later) | Skills-based tracks for SHS (TVL) and TESDA graduates | More of their graduates placed in jobs |
| Industry associations such as IBPAP (later) | Introductions to member firms and industry credibility | A source of trainees for member companies' entry-level roles |

*Table 2.14. Strategic Partners and Mutual Benefits*

Under the EBET Framework Act (Republic Act No. 12063), companies that run enterprise-based training can get tax incentives. Hakbang can use this as a selling point when signing employers to run train-to-hire tracks.

### **D.6 Expansion Strategy**

After winning the beachhead, Hakbang will expand to nearby segments that can use the same platform with small changes.

| Order | Next customer | Why next | What changes |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1 | Underemployed young workers in Metro Manila | Same employers, same roles, similar age and phone habits | Evening and weekend training schedules |
| 2 | SHS (TVL) and TESDA graduates | Many entry roles do not need a degree | TESDA-aligned tracks; skills-based matching instead of degree-based |
| 3 | Same segments in regional IT-BPM hubs (Cebu, Davao, Iloilo, Bacolod) | IT-BPM is growing outside Metro Manila | Local employer partners and university tie-ups |
| 4 | Informal workers | Highest need under SDG 8 | Work with LGU PESOs; simpler app and offline help desks |
| 5 | Career shifters aged 30 and above | Large group with work experience to build on | Recognition of past experience; shorter training tracks |

*Table 2.15. Expansion Sequence for Customer Segments*

On the employer side, Hakbang will move from BPO and IT-BPM firms to retail and food chains, logistics and warehouse companies, tech startups, and MSMEs with 50 or more workers.

### **D.7 Scaling Approach**

* **Network effects.** Each new employer brings more training tracks, which attracts more job seekers. More qualified job seekers then attract more employers. This two-sided network becomes harder to copy as it grows.  
* **Smarter matching over time.** The matching engine starts as rules-based scoring. As hires and retention data accumulate, it will move to a machine learning model, which improves matches as the platform grows.  
* **Low cost to add users.** Hakbang is a cloud-based progressive web app, so adding users and regions costs little compared with opening physical offices. Regional expansion needs local employer partners and university tie-ups, not new infrastructure.  
* **Repeatable partner playbook.** The process used to sign the first universities and PESOs becomes a standard package (onboarding steps, promotional materials, and placement reports) that can be reused in each new city.  
* **New revenue as the base grows.** Once the job seeker base is large enough, Hakbang can add paid featured listings for employers on top of the success fee, while keeping the platform free for job seekers.

### **A.3 Needs and Problems**

The two sides of the market do not meet well. Job seekers need skills and a first stable job, while companies are willing to train but struggle to find the right people to train.

|  | Job seekers (end users) | Employers (paying customer) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Core need** | A clear path from training to a formal job with benefits | Job-ready hires at a lower cost per successful hire |
| **Problems** | "No experience" rejections; fake job posts and scams; unpaid training with no job at the end; limited access to training | Many applicants but few qualified; manual screening; training money wasted on people who quit or fail |
| **What they value** | Legit, verified companies; visible progress; training with a job offer | Pre-screened, pre-matched trainees; higher retention; pay-for-results pricing |

*Table 3.5. Needs and Problems of Job Seekers and Employers*

The problem is backed by data. In March 2026, PSA reported 5.0% unemployment and 12.3% underemployment, and about 753,000 of 5.76 million employed youth (13.1%) were underemployed. Only 28.6% of establishments with 10 or more workers gave job-related training in 2023 (PSA ISLE), so most workers must find and pay for training on their own. The IT-BPM industry spends about P1.4 billion a year on talent development, yet still lists the supply of employable talent as a main challenge for 2026\.

## **B. Market Size and Trends**

### **B.1 Market Size: TAM, SAM, SOM**

Our TAM comes directly from the Target Customer paper. The SAM and SOM figures are new estimates built on the same logic, and every percentage marked "assumption" will be checked against CHED data and our interviews.

| Item | Value | Basis |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| College graduates per year (Philippines) | \~796,000 | SY 2019-2020 graduates, Congressional Policy and Budget Research Department |
| Share from Metro Manila | 20% \= \~159,200 per year | Assumption |
| Graduates 0-2 years out | x2 \= \~318,400 | Two graduating batches |
| Share still job-hunting or mismatched | 40% \= \~127,400 end users | Assumption |
| Revenue per hire | P5,000 | Assumption: employer success fee per hire |

*Table 3.8. Market Size Inputs and Assumptions*

**TAM (Total Addressable Market):** All fresh graduates in Metro Manila who are jobless or in jobs unrelated to their course: about 127,400 people, or roughly P637 million per year (127,400 x P5,000). Even if we reach only a small part of this, the beachhead is big enough to build a business on, but small enough for a student team to focus on and dominate first.

**SAM (Serviceable Available Market):** The part of the TAM we can serve with our current product. Hakbang starts with entry-level IT-BPM train-to-hire roles and an app-based service, so we count only graduates who fit those roles and can be reached through our channels. We assume about 50% of the TAM qualifies: roughly 63,700 people, or about P318.5 million per year (assumption).

**SOM (Serviceable Obtainable Market):** The share of the SAM we expect to win in our first three years, given a student team, a small number of employer partners, and growth driven by word of mouth and university career offices. Assuming one to two BPO partners in Year 1, which grows with batch-to-batch referrals:

| Year | Share of SAM | Successful hires | Revenue (at P5,000 per hire) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Year 1** | 0.5% | \~319 | \~P1.6 million |
| **Year 2** | 1.5% | \~956 | \~P4.8 million |
| **Year 3** | 3.0% | \~1,911 | \~P9.6 million |

*Table 3.9. Serviceable Obtainable Market by Year*

As a sanity check, one mid-size BPO like Carla's fills 40 to 60 seats a month, or roughly 480 to 720 a year. Year 1 therefore needs only a small number of partner companies, and Year 3 needs a modest network of them. The SOM is small by design, which keeps the plan realistic while the TAM shows room to grow.

![][image10]

*Figure 3.1. Hakbang TAM, SAM, and SOM Funnel*

Figure 3.1 shows how Hakbang narrows its market from the total opportunity to what it expects to win. The TAM is about 127,400 fresh graduates in Metro Manila who are jobless or working in jobs unrelated to their course, worth roughly P637 million a year at the P5,000 success fee. The SAM is the half of that group (about 63,700 graduates, or P318.5 million a year) who fit entry-level IT-BPM train-to-hire roles and can be reached through Hakbang’s app and channel partners. The SOM is the share Hakbang expects to win in its first three years: 0.5% of the SAM in Year 1 (about 319 hires), 1.5% in Year 2 (about 956 hires), and 3.0% in Year 3 (about 1,911 hires). Three inputs are still assumptions that the 20 planned interviews and CHED data will check: the 20% Metro Manila share of national graduates, the 40% of graduates who are still job-hunting or mismatched, and the 50% of the TAM that qualifies as the SAM. The SOM is kept small by design, since a student team with a few employer partners and word-of-mouth growth can only fill so many seats, and it stays realistic because a single mid-size BPO like Carla’s already fills 480 to 720 seats a year.

**Growth beyond the beachhead** Expanding to underemployed workers, SHS/TESDA graduates, regional IT-BPM hubs, and later informal workers and career shifters would widen the TAM well beyond Metro Manila fresh graduates, and adding retail, logistics and MSME employers adds more paying customers per user.

### **B.2 Market Trends**

1. **Persistent underemployment.** PSA's March 2026 data shows unemployment easing to 5.0%, but underemployment remains at 12.3%, and 13.1% of employed youth are underemployed. Jobs exist, but many are not stable or well matched, which is the gap Hakbang targets.  
2. **A training gap in the workforce.** Only 28.6% of establishments with 10 or more workers gave job-related training in 2023\. Most workers must upskill on their own, which makes company-sponsored train-to-hire tracks valuable.  
3. **A growing IT-BPM industry with a talent supply problem.** The industry has passed the US\$40 billion revenue mark and is targeting close to 2 million workers in 2026\. It spends about P1.4 billion a year on talent development, yet employable talent supply is still a main challenge. A recent report also notes that revenue growth is outpacing job creation, which increases pressure on employers to find and train efficiently.  
4. **Mobile-first, digitally ready job seekers.** Fresh graduates already search and apply on their phones, so an app-based matching and tracking service needs little handholding.  
5. **Rising demand for trust and transparency.** Scam postings and training programs with no job at the end make verified employers and outcome tracking a competitive need, not an extra feature.  
6. **Skills-based hiring.** Many entry roles do not require a degree, which supports our later expansion to SHS and TESDA graduates.

## **C. Competition and Competitive Edge**

### **C.1 SWOT Analysis**

Section B showed that demand for train-to-hire exists: youth underemployment remains at 12.3%, only 28.6% of establishments gave job-related training, and IT-BPM still lists employable talent supply as a main challenge (PSA, 2026; Manila Times, 2026). Before comparing Hakbang with other platforms, the team asks whether it is positioned to capture that demand. The table below lists Hakbang’s internal strengths and weaknesses and the external opportunities and threats from Chapter II (Industry), Chapter III, B.2 (Market Trends), and the PESTLE and Five Forces analyses in Chapter II, A.8.

| :---- | :---- |
| Train-to-hire in one flow | Job boards end at the listing and learning sites end at the certificate. Hakbang follows the trainee to a signed contract (Ch. IV, A.3). |
| Verified employers only | Fake job posts are a documented problem. DOLE has repeatedly warned about fake social media job pages (Inquirer, 2019), and its Bureau of Local Employment has urged jobseekers to verify offers with PESOs (SunStar, n.d.). |
| Pay-for-results pricing | Agencies typically charge 15% to 25% of the first-year salary (9cv9, 2026). At an illustrative P20,000 monthly salary, that is P36,000 to P60,000, against Hakbang’s P5,000 (our computation). |
| Free for job seekers | Paid course platforms charge learners, and TESDA Online is free but has no employer commitment attached (TESDA, n.d.). |
| Asset-light model | Partner companies supply the training content, so Hakbang builds no courses (Ch. II, B.4). |
| Founder-market fit | The team belongs to the beachhead segment. For example, DLSU’s jobs and internships Facebook group listed over 16,000 members (ICPA, n.d.). |

**Strategic implications**

Matching strengths and weaknesses with opportunities and threats gives four priorities, each carried into later sections:

| Weaknesses | Borrow credibility from universities and PESOs, and use pilot hire and retention data to build a track record (Ch. IV, A.6). | Validate the fee through interviews and confirm the DOLE license before launch (Ch. III, A.4; Ch. II, A.6). |

*Table 3.14. Strategic Implications of SWOT Analysis*

Hakbang’s strengths sit where existing options are weakest: trust, outcomes, and employer risk. Job boards leave screening to the employer, learning platforms offer no job, and agencies charge a large percentage of salary. Section C.2 maps these competitors, C.3 compares them on pricing, distribution, and promotion, C.4 turns the comparison into Hakbang’s differentiators, and C.5 sets out responses to the threats listed above.

### **C.2 Competitor Landscape**

Our target customers currently get jobs through job boards, social media groups, job fairs, referrals, and agencies, and they get training from separate programs. We found a few platforms that combine company-sponsored training, matching, progress tracking and a hiring commitment in one place. Our competition is therefore mostly indirect, plus a few direct players that partly overlap.

**Direct competitors** (platforms that match job seekers to employers and offer some screening, assessment or upskilling features):

* Kalibrr  
* PhilJobNet (DOLE's public employment portal)  
* Job-matching and recruitment features inside TESDA and LGU PESO programs

**Indirect competitors** (alternatives our customers use to solve the same problem):

* Job boards and networks: JobStreet and LinkedIn  
* Facebook job groups and referrals  
* School job fairs and PESO job fairs  
* Recruitment and staffing agencies  
* Online learning platforms: TESDA Online, Coursera and Udemy (offers training with no job attached)  
* Employers' own career pages and in-house training academies

| Competitor | Strength | Weakness | Pricing | Distribution | Promotion |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Jobstreet | Largest local job board, strong brand, many listings | Thousands of applicants per post; no training or progress tracking; the "no experience" filter remains; scam posts possible | Free Lite ad for up to 30 days (Jobstreet, n.d.-a). Paid Basic, Branded, and Premium ads vary by role and location; third parties report about ₱6,720 for Basic and ₱10,976 for Premium per ad. | Employer portal and app; ads go out through the website, social media, and email alerts (Jobstreet, n.d.-b). | Free job posting for employers (Philstar, 2024); upsells for visibility and priority listing (Jobstreet, n.d.-c). |
| LinkedIn | Professional network, employer branding, recruiter tools | Fresh graduates have thin networks and profiles; no training or hiring commitment | One free job at a time; paid promotion on a flexible daily budget (LinkedIn, n.d.). Recruiter Lite costs about US\$170 a month (Juicebox, 2026). | Global professional network on web and mobile; automated job targeting to relevant candidates (LinkedIn, n.d.). | Paid promotion across LinkedIn and job-seeker emails (LinkedIn, n.d.). |

Employers buy subscriptions of up to 5 job slots for 1 to 12 months, with custom plans through sales. A third-party listing shows an SME starting price of ₱19,365. | Web and mobile app focused on white-collar roles; posts go to LinkedIn, Google, and Indeed in one click (Kalibrr, 2026). | Employer branding, a "Kalibrr vs. Jobstreet" page, a Top 50 Employers ranking, and career-advice blogs (Kalibrr, 2026). |

This cell is partly our inference, so we will check it with PESO officers. |

Fake pages are common, and DOLE has warned jobseekers about fake social media job pages (Inquirer, 2019). |

This cell is partly our inference, so check it in employer interviews. |

Coursera Plus is about \$59 a month or \$399 a year, and Udemy lists courses from about \$9.99 to \$199.99 (MentorCruise, 2026). | Self-paced web platforms. IT-BPM spends about P1.4 billion a year on talent development (Manila Times, 2026), and only 28.6% of establishments gave job-related training in 2023 (PSA, n.d.). | Delivered by the employer for its own hires only. | Employer career pages and referrals. This is our inference, so confirm it in interviews. |

*Table 3.15. Comparative Analysis of Competitors*

### **C.4 Differentiators and Competitive Edge**

1. **Train-to-hire in one flow.** Job seekers train under a company's own program with a formal employment contract at the end. Job boards list jobs and learning platforms give courses, but neither connects the two.  
2. **Verified employers only.** We screen partner companies through an employer verification process, which answers scam fears and the "free training with no job" problem Bea faced (Ch. II, C.4).  
3. **Smart matching using a Living Profile.** Skills, school, location and preferences feed a matching algorithm, with AI used for skill-gap detection and recommendations. Employers get pre-matched trainees instead of hundreds of unfit applicants.  
4. **Progress tracking and employer endorsements.** Job seekers see each step and earn verified endorsements that carry over to future applications. Employers see who is serious.  
5. **Pay-for-results pricing.** Employers pay mainly a success fee per hire, so they take on little upfront risk. This is a strong selling point against agencies and job boards that charge regardless of outcome.  
6. **Free for job seekers.** Costs are no barrier for our beachhead users, and we do not make the training ourselves, which keeps our model asset-light.  
7. **Founder-market fit.** As college students ourselves, we can reach fresh graduates through batchmates, org pages and career offices faster than most established players.

**Competitive edge summary:** Better outcomes for both sides (a guaranteed path from training to a formal job), higher trust through verification, and lower employer risk through success-based pricing, supported by AI-assisted matching.

### **C.5 Risks and How We Respond**

* **Big job boards add training features.** The CEO is in charge of managing this risk. We will respond by building employer relationships and a verified outcomes record early, which are harder to copy than features.  
* **Employers keep their own pipelines.** The CEO is also in charge of managing this risk. We address it by proving a lower cost per successful hire in pilots with one or two BPO partners.  
* **Low-quality or scam partners damage trust.** The COO is responsible for managing this risk. We respond with strict employer verification before any partner goes live.  
* **The P5,000 success fee turns out too high or too low.** The CFO is responsible for managing this risk. We will test willingness to pay in employer interviews and adjust the pricing model.

# **Chapter IV. Market Plan**

---

## **A. Overall Marketing Strategy**

### **A.1 Segmentation**

We split job seekers into five groups: fresh college graduates, underemployed young workers, SHS and TESDA graduates, informal workers, and career shifters. We split employers by industry: IT-BPM firms and GCCs, retail and logistics companies, and MSMEs.

### **A.2 Targeting**

We start with fresh college graduates in Metro Manila who are 0 to 2 years out of school and are jobless or in jobs unrelated to their course. This group scored 24 out of 25 in our matrix. On the paying side, we start with talent acquisition, HR, and L\&D leads at mid-size BPO and IT-BPM firms that fill 40 to 60 entry-level seats a month, like our persona Carla.

### **A.3 Positioning**

**For job seekers:** For fresh graduates who keep hearing "no experience," Hakbang is a train-to-hire hub that links them to verified employers who train them and commit to hiring those who pass. A job board ends at the listing and a course site ends at the certificate. Hakbang follows the trainee up to a signed job contract.

**For employers:** For HR and L\&D managers who lose training money on people who quit, Hakbang sends pre-screened, pre-matched trainees, and the company pays only when a trainee gets hired.

### **A.4 Branding and Desired Image**

* **Name and tagline.** "Hakbang" means "step." Our tagline, "Isang hakbang papunta sa trabaho" (one step toward a job), tells users we move them forward one stage at a time.  
* **Desired image.** We want job seekers to see Hakbang as the safe, legit option in a feed full of scam posts. We want employers to see us as a low-risk hiring partner that gets paid on results.  
* **Voice.** We speak friendly Taglish to job seekers on social media and plain, data-backed English to employers.  
* **Trust markers.** Each partner carries a "Verified Employer" badge, each training track shows how many trainees that company has hired, and we share real hire stories with the trainee's consent.

### **A.5 Customer Acquisition**

We sign employers first. A job seeker who signs up and finds no open training tracks will not come back, so we need one or two BPO pilot partners before we open sign-ups. We reach these partners through faculty and alumni referrals, LinkedIn outreach, and industry events. Once tracks are open, we bring in job seekers through university career offices, student organizations, graduate Facebook groups, and batchmate referrals.

### **A.6 Growth Strategy**

We grow in four phases. The hire targets follow the SOM in Chapter III.

| Phase | Timing | Focus | Target |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Pilot | Year 1, first half | 1 to 2 BPO partners; DLSU and 2 to 3 nearby universities; first batch of 20 to 30 trainees | Prove cost per hire and 90-day retention |
| Launch | Year 1, second half | 3 to 5 partners; career offices in about 10 Metro Manila schools | About 319 hires in Year 1 |
| Expand | Year 2 | More IT-BPM and GCC partners; add underemployed young workers (Segment B) | About 956 hires |
| Scale | Year 3 | IT-BPM hubs outside Metro Manila; add SHS and TESDA graduates; add retail and logistics employers | About 1,911 hires |

*Table 4.1. Growth Phases and Hire Targets*

## **B. Pricing**

### **B.1 Pricing Model**

Hakbang charges one side of the market. Job seekers pay nothing. Employers pay a success fee only after a trainee passes training and signs an employment contract. Employers in our research named wasted training money as a main pain, so we chose a model where they carry little upfront risk.

| Item | Who pays | Price | Notes |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Account, Living Profile, matching, and training tracks | Job seeker | Free | Stays free at all stages |
| Standard success fee | Employer | P5,000 per hire | Billed after the hire signs a contract (assumption) |
| Pilot rate | Employer | P2,500 per hire | First batch only; lowers the risk of trying us (assumption) |
| Volume rate | Employer | P4,000 per hire | For partners with more than 30 hires in a quarter (assumption) |
| Employer Pro dashboard | Employer | P10,000 per month | Optional, from Year 2: hiring analytics, branded track page, bulk interview scheduling (assumption) |

*Table 4.3. Hakbang Price Model*

### **B.2 How the Model Answers Each Pricing Option**

* **Subscription fees.** None in Year 1\. From Year 2, large partners can add the optional Employer Pro plan.  
* **One-time payments.** The success fee is a one-time charge per hire. We charge no setup or listing fee.  
* **Freemium.** Job seekers get the full service for free. Employers can post training tracks and view matched trainees for free and pay only per hire.

### **B.3 Billing and Testing the Price**

We bill employers once a month for the hires made that month, with 30-day payment terms. At the standard fee, our Year 1 target of about 319 hires brings in about P1.6 million; pilot rates will pull the real figure lower. The P5,000 fee is still an assumption. In our 20 interviews we will ask employers what they spend per entry-level hire today, including training, and adjust the fee to sit below that cost.

## **C. Sales Tactics**

### **C.1 Employer Sales Funnel**

The five founders handle sales in Year 1\. We sell to the person who owns the hiring budget: the talent acquisition lead, HR manager, or L\&D manager.

| Stage | What we do | Target (assumption) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Prospect | List 50 BPOs, GCCs, and mid-size firms in Metro Manila from industry member lists, LinkedIn, and alumni contacts | 50 companies |
| Contact | Send LinkedIn messages and emails; ask faculty and alumni for warm introductions | 20 meetings |
| Discovery call | Ask about hiring volume, cost per hire, and attrition in the first 3 months | 10 interested firms |
| Pilot proposal | Offer one batch of 20 trainees at the pilot rate, with clear success measures | 3 to 5 pilots |
| Pilot | Run the training track and send the employer a weekly progress report | At least 70% of trainees hired |
| Contract | Sign a 12-month partner agreement at the standard or volume rate | 3 to 5 partners in Year 1 |

*Table 4.4. Employer Sales Funnel and Targets*

### **C.2 Job Seeker Funnel**

**Awareness → Sign up → Complete Living Profile → Matched to a track → Finish training → Hired**

* **Lead generation.** Campus career talks, career office referral links, student org partners, graduate Facebook groups, and a batchmate referral code.  
* **Fast sign-up.** A new user can build a basic Living Profile in under 5 minutes, then add skills over time.  
* **Proof up front.** Each track shows the "Verified Employer" badge, the written hiring commitment, and past hire counts. This answers the scam fear that Bea raised.  
* **Keeping trainees on track.** We send reminders through Messenger, SMS, and email, and we group trainees into small batches so they push each other to finish.

### **C.3 Closing Employer Deals**

* **Pilot pricing.** The first batch costs half the standard fee.  
* **Results report.** After each pilot we show the employer its cost per hire and 90-day retention next to its old numbers.  
* **Case studies.** With permission, we use each pilot's results to pitch the next employer.  
* **Replacement guarantee.** Section D explains how we cover hires who leave early.

## **D. Service and Warranty Policies**

Hakbang sells a service, so it has no product returns. Our replacement guarantee and fee credit serve as the return policy for employers.

### **D.1 For Employers**

* **No hire, no fee.** Employers pay only for trainees who sign a job contract.  
* **90-day replacement guarantee.** If a Hakbang hire resigns or gets let go within 90 days, we give the employer a free replacement from the next batch. If no fit comes up within 60 days, we credit 50% of the fee to its next hire (assumption).  
* **Partner agreement.** Each partner signs an agreement that lists the training track, number of slots, hiring commitment, fee, and data rules.  
* **Support.** Each partner gets one Hakbang contact person, a reply within one business day, and a monthly hiring report.

### **D.2 For Job Seekers**

* **Free, with no hidden fees.** If a partner asks a trainee for money, we remove that partner from Hakbang.  
* **Hiring commitment.** Each track carries the employer's written commitment to hire trainees who pass. If a partner breaks it, we suspend the partner and move the affected trainees to other tracks first.  
* **Report button.** Users can report scams, abuse, or false job details. We review each report within 48 hours.  
* **Help desk.** Users reach us through in-app chat and Messenger, and we reply within 24 hours.  
* **Data privacy.** We follow the Data Privacy Act of 2012 (RA 10173). Trainees choose which employers see their profile, and they can delete their account at any time.

### **D.3 Technical Support**

Users and employers can report bugs in the app. We fix issues that block sign-up, training, or hiring first, and we post planned maintenance at least 2 days ahead.

## **A. Development Status and Tasks**

### **A.1 Where the Product Stands**

Hakbang is at the concept and validation stage. We have defined the business model, personas, feature set, and technology stack (Ch. II, B and C). The team is drafting a prototype of the main screens for the course MVP requirement, but no production software exists yet. Under our launch strategy, building starts once the 20 interviews confirm the pain points and at least one employer agrees to a pilot (Ch. II, D.3).

### **A.2 Development Approach Using the SDLC**

We follow the System Development Life Cycle (SDLC) to move from idea to release. We use an iterative version of it: planning and requirements happen once, then design, development, and testing repeat in two-week sprints, with a demo to the whole team at the end of each sprint.

![][image13]

*Figure 5.1. Hakbang Development Using the SDLC*

| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1\. Planning | Define the problem, beachhead, business model, pricing, and budget | All five founders; CFO on the budget | Course instructor/faculty mentor | Sep to Nov 2026 | Done | First and second pass business plan, Lean Canvas |
| 2\. Requirements analysis | Interview 20 respondents (12 job seekers, 6 employers, 2 partners); write user stories; list legal requirements under the Data Privacy Act, NPC rules, and DOLE rules | COO (led the interviews); CEO (employer and partner interviews); COO and CFO (compliance checklist) | 12 job seekers, 6 employer HR/L\&D leads, 2 partners (career office or PESO); legal counsel | Nov 2026 to Jan 8, 2027 | In progress | Validated feature list, fee, and compliance checklist |
| 3\. Design | User flows, wireframes, data model, system architecture, privacy notice and consent text | CTO (data model, architecture); CMO (user flows, wireframes) | Interview respondents who review the wireframes; legal counsel (privacy notice and consent text) | Jan 11 to 24, 2027 | Planned | Approved wireframes and project shell |
| 4\. Development | Build sign-up, Living Profile, employer dashboard, track posting, verification admin view, matching, and progress tracker in sprints | CTO (lead); the other founders and the freelance developer as backup | Pilot partner employer (reviews the track posting flow) | Jan 25 to Mar 14, 2027 | Planned | Feature-complete pilot build |
| 5\. Testing | Feature tests in every sprint; usability tests with 10 to 15 recent graduates; security check of HTTPS, role-based access, and consent records | COO (coordinates tests); CTO (security check) | 10–15 recent graduates; pilot partner | Mar 8 to 28, 2027 | Planned | Test report and fix list |
| 6\. Deployment | Release the pilot build, onboard the first partner, open sign-ups to the pilot cohort | CTO (release); COO (partner onboarding); CEO (partner agreement); CMO (opens sign-ups) | Pilot employer, first trainee cohort, university career office or PESO | Mar 29 to Apr 5, 2027 | Planned | Live pilot release |
| 7\. Maintenance | Fix bugs, watch usage and costs, ship the launch features in later sprints | CTO (bugs, cloud costs); COO (help desk); part-time developer from Months 7–12 | Employers, job seekers, NPC (if there's an incident) | Apr 2027 onward | Planned | Launch release, then later versions |

*Table 5.1. Hakbang SDLC Phases*

Four choices keep the first build small enough for a student team:

* **Web first, mobile app later.** Year 1 runs only on the progressive web app, which works in any phone browser, so the pilot needs no app store listing, fees, or review. If we reach the Year 1 milestone (at least 3 active employer partners and about 319 hires by December 2027), we build the Android and iOS apps in Year 2 from the same code (team assumption).  
* **Managed services.** Supabase and Vercel handle login, storage, and hosting, so the team writes product features and not server code.  
* **Rules first, machine learning later.** The first matching engine uses a scoring rule over skills, location, and schedule. It moves to a machine learning model once we have hire and retention data (Ch. II, D.7).  
* **Manual first, automated later.** Employer verification and track onboarding start as a checklist in a simple admin view. We automate them once the process works.

## **B. Difficulties and Risks**

A two-sided platform fails if employers do not sign. A platform that holds personal data fails if it loses trust. The tables below list the hurdles we expect, rated by the team for likelihood and impact, with a mitigation and a fallback plan for each.

### **B.1 Technical Challenges**

| Risk | Rating (likelihood / impact) | Owner | Support | Mitigation | Fallback plan |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Weak matches because data is thin | Medium / High | CTO | COO reviews pilot matches by hand | Use clear rules-based scoring; review every pilot match by hand; log outcomes to train a model later | The team builds pilot shortlists by hand while the engine improves |
| Small team with limited coding time | High / Medium | CEO | CTO reports the schedule, and the CFO approves freelancer cost | Limit the pilot to five core features; use managed services; add a 15% schedule buffer | Hire a freelance developer from two or three collected quotes |
| AI errors and bias, such as a wrong resume reading or ranking applicants lower because of their school | Medium / High | CTO | COO audits the AI outputs | Users review every AI-filled field; school and name are not ranking factors; log AI outputs; set a monthly API spending cap | Turn off AI filling and use a plain form |
| Scalability and cost spikes | Medium / Medium | CTO | CFO approves plan upgrades | Move to paid plans before the pilot (Vercel's free plan is non-commercial, and Supabase's free plan pauses idle projects) (Makerkit, 2026; MetaCTO, n.d.); set usage alerts | Upgrade the plan or move the PostgreSQL database to another host, since the data uses a standard format |
| Data breach | Low / High | CTO | COO notifies the NPC and affected users within 72 hours | HTTPS, role-based access, database access rules per user, monthly backups | Follow an incident plan: contain the breach and notify the NPC and affected users within 72 hours |
| Poor mobile signal and low-end phones | Medium / Medium | CTO | CMO supports with Messenger channels | Keep pages light, compress images, test on mid-range Android phones | Send key alerts by SMS and Messenger; add offline help desks later (Ch. II, D.6) |

*Table 5.5. Technical Challenges, Mitigation, and Fallback Plans*

### **B.2 External Bottlenecks**

| Bottleneck | Rating (likelihood / impact) | Owner | Support | Mitigation | Fallback plan |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| DOLE recruitment license | Medium / High | COO | legal counsel supports | Ask DOLE before the pilot whether a matching platform needs a license (Ch. II, A.6) | Position Hakbang as a software tool in which the employer makes every hiring decision, or partner with a licensed agency while we apply |
| NPC registration for automated profiling | High / Medium | COO as DPO owns it | – | Register the system and name a data protection officer before the pilot (NPC, 2022\) | Delay AI ranking features until registration clears |
| Cold start: no tracks when job seekers arrive | High / High | CEO | COO enters the partner's track | Build the employer dashboard first; enter the pilot partner's track for them; open sign-ups only after tracks are live | Widen outreach to MSMEs with 50 or more workers |
| Vendor dependence on Supabase, Vercel, and the AI provider | Low / Medium | CTO | – | Export backups monthly; avoid vendor-only features where a standard one exists | Switch to another PostgreSQL host, hosting service, or LLM provider |
| A fake or unfit employer passes verification | Low / High | COO | CEO handles suspension and DOLE reporting | Check SEC or DTI registration, BIR Form 2303, and the business permit (PhilJobNet, n.d.); review track terms; sign a partner agreement | Suspend the partner, move trainees to other tracks, and report the case to DOLE |
| App store review delays | Medium / Low | CTO | – | Submit early; the web app works without a store listing (Choicely, 2026\) | Keep users on the web app until approval |
| Year 1 milestone not reached | Medium / Medium | CEO | CFO tracks the monthly numbers; the board decides on the fallback | Track active partners and hires every month against the Year 1 targets | Stay web-only in Year 2 and put the mobile app budget into the core service |

## **E. Proprietary Issues**

Hakbang's value lies in its name, software, matching rules, and data. Table 5.9 lists each asset and how Philippine law protects it. We will confirm these steps with a lawyer before launch, using the legal review budget in Table 5.8.

| Asset | How it is protected |
| :---- | :---- |
| Name, logo, and tagline (“Hakbang,” “Isang hakbang papunta sa trabaho,” \#UnangHakbang, the “Verified Employer” badge) | Trademark registration with the Intellectual Property Office of the Philippines (IPOPHL), filed online through eTMfile and valid for 10 years (Triple i Consulting, n.d.) |
| Software code, app screens, and written content | Copyright attaches automatically on creation under the Intellectual Property Code, Republic Act No. 8293, and covers computer programs; depositing the software gives a public record useful in a dispute (NDV Law, n.d.-b) |
| Matching rules, scoring weights, and employer lists and pricing | Protected as trade secrets only if the company takes active steps to keep them secret (NDV Law, n.d.-b) |
| Job seeker data in the Living Profile | Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10173); the job seeker owns their data, and Hakbang is the personal information controller |
| NPC registration | NPC Circular 2022-04 requires registration of systems that process sensitive personal information of 1,000 or more people (NPC, 2022), and any system involving automated decision-making or profiling must be registered in all instances (NDV Law, n.d.-a) |
| Training content, endorsements, and employer logos | Owned by the employers that create them |
| Third-party tools and AI provider | Terms of service of Supabase, Vercel, the AI provider, and the app stores |

*Table 5.9. Proprietary Assets and Protection Plan*

The pitch "Grab for train-to-hire" in Chapter II, B.5 uses another company's brand, so we keep it to internal and classroom use and leave it out of public marketing.

# **Chapter VI. Manufacturing and Operations Plan**

---

Hakbang does not manufacture goods. Its "production" is a service: matching job seekers to employer training and following each trainee to a signed contract.

## **A. Operating Cycle**

### **A.1 The Four Steps**

The standard operating cycle has four steps: get the inputs, produce the service, sell it, and collect payment. Figure 6.1 and Table 6.1 show how each step works for Hakbang.

![][image15]

*Figure 6.1. Hakbang Operating Cycle*

| Standard step | What it means for Hakbang | Who does it | Typical time (assumption) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1\. Order raw materials | Our inputs are employer tracks and job seekers. We sign and verify employers, take in their tracks, and recruit job seekers through career offices, student organizations, and referrals. | CEO and COO (employers); CMO (job seekers) | 2 to 4 weeks to sign and verify a new partner |
| 2\. Produce the service | Smart Matching builds a shortlist for each track. Trainees complete the employer's modules while the Progress Tracker records results and endorsements. | Platform, technical lead, partner trainers | 2 to 6 weeks per track |
| 3\. Sell | Trainees who pass the final assessment receive a formal job offer. The employer confirms the hire in the dashboard. | Partner employer, COO | 1 week after the track ends |
| 4\. Collect payment | We bill the employer at month end for all hires that month, with 30-day terms. The 90-day replacement guarantee then starts. | CFO | 30 to 60 days after the hire |

*Table 6.1. Hakbang Operating Cycle*

From the day a track opens to the day we collect cash takes about 2 to 4 months. That gap matters for cash flow: in Year 1 we pay cloud, AI, and legal costs before the first success fees arrive. The financial plan will cover this gap with founders' funds, startup competition prizes, and the half-price pilot fees.

### **A.2 Value Chain**

Porter's value chain splits a business into primary activities, which create and deliver value, and support activities, which make the primary ones possible (Porter, 1985). Figure 6.2 maps Hakbang's activities.

![][image16]

*Figure 6.2. Hakbang Value Chain*

| Activity | Hakbang's version | Source of advantage |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Inbound logistics | Employer sign-up, document checks, track intake; job seeker sign-up and consent | Verification builds the trust that job boards lack |
| Operations | Living Profile, Smart Matching, AI skill-gap check, progress tracking, endorsements | Pre-matched trainees lower employer screening time |
| Outbound logistics | Shortlists sent to employers, hire confirmation, monthly hiring reports, aggregate placement reports for schools | Employers see results in one dashboard |
| Marketing and sales | Direct B2B sales to HR and L\&D leads; \#UnangHakbang campaign, campus events, referrals | Founders belong to the beachhead and reach it at low cost |
| Service | 90-day replacement guarantee, help desk, report button, 48-hour scam review | Lower risk for employers and safety for job seekers |
| Firm infrastructure | Corporate registration, finance and billing, legal and data privacy compliance | Compliance with RA 10173 and DOLE rules protects the brand |
| Human resource management | Founder roles, part-time hires, volunteer HR mentors for mock interviews | A lean team keeps fixed costs low |
| Technology development | PWA, matching engine, AI features, admin tools | Hire and retention data improve matching over time |
| Procurement | Cloud hosting, AI API, SMS and email services, legal review | Pay-as-you-go services keep spending tied to use |

*Table 6.2. Hakbang Value Chain Activities*

The strongest links are inbound logistics (verification) and operations (matching). These are where Hakbang creates value that competitors do not, so they get most of our time and money in Year 1\.

## **B. Geographic Location**

### **B.1 Where We Operate**

Hakbang runs online, so it needs no plant or warehouse. In Year 1 the team works from the De La Salle University campus on Taft Avenue, Manila, and from home. The platform runs on Vercel and on Supabase's Singapore region, close to Philippine users (Ch. II, C.3). Once we incorporate, we will register a business address in Manila, at a co-working space or a campus incubator such as DLSU Animo Labs if we are accepted.

### **B.2 Why This Location**

We chose Manila because Hakbang has to sit close to both sides of its market. Our job seekers study in the universities along the LRT-1 line, and our paying customers hire in business districts a short ride away. The founders also study on Taft Avenue, so working from campus costs nothing and keeps the team together. We considered starting in Cebu, which is already in our v3.0 roadmap, but our university ties and pilot partner leads are in Manila, so Cebu waits until Year 3 (Table 5.7).

* **Near our job seekers.** Taft Avenue sits close to several universities, and the LRT-1 connects the area to other Manila campuses. Career offices and student organizations, our main job seeker channels, are within reach.  
* **Near our paying customers.** Metro Manila holds the main IT-BPM business districts, including Makati, Ortigas, and Bonifacio Global City, where our target BPOs and GCCs hire.  
* **Skilled labor.** Computer science and business students in the area can fill part-time developer and associate roles.  
* **Low-latency hosting.** A Singapore data center keeps the app fast for users in the Philippines.

### **B.3 Tax, Zoning, and Labor Cost Factors**

* **BMBE Act (RA 9178).** A business with total assets of P3 million or less, excluding land, can register as a Barangay Micro Business Enterprise and earn an income tax exemption on its operating income. Hakbang's Year 1 assets are mainly laptops and software subscriptions, well below the limit. We would still pay other taxes, such as percentage tax, and keep proper books.  
* **Innovative Startup Act (RA 11337).** The law created the Philippine Startup Development Program, under which DTI, DOST, and DICT offer grants, subsidies, and other support to qualified startups.  
* **Zoning.** A software service raises no zoning issues. We need a business permit from the city where we register.  
* **Labor cost.** Founders work without salary in Year 1\. Part-time student hires cost less than full-time staff, and remote work saves on office rent.

These factors make Manila a cheap place to start. The BMBE exemption removes income tax in 2027, and with no rent and no salaried staff, Year 1 cash costs stay near P60,000 a month even at year end (Table 9.6). The CFO files the BMBE and tax registrations, and the team applies for startup grants after the pilot, when it has results to show.

## **C. Facilities and Improvements**

### **C.1 Current Facilities**

Hakbang starts without a leased office because its service is software, and every peso saved on space can go to the paid cloud plans the pilot needs. Platforms like Vercel and Supabase are the one cost we commit to from day one. Their free plans are non-commercial or pause idle projects (Ch. V, B.1), which a live pilot with real trainees cannot accept. The five founder-owned laptops and the test phones cover development and testing, so we spend no cash on equipment. We chose campus spaces and home work over a rented room because the team already meets on campus, and a lease would add a fixed monthly cost before the first success fee arrives.

### **C.2 Future Capacity**

We added facilities only when the work requires them. In the pilot, nothing changes: one or two partners and 20 to 30 trainees can be handled remotely. In Year 2, with about 956 hires and the first employees, partner meetings and trainee onboarding need a place to meet in person, so we plan to rent 3 to 4 co-working seats in Manila. At about P5,000 per seat per month (assumption), that gives the P15,000 to P20,000 shown. In Year 3, regional partners and about 1,911 hires justify a presence in one regional hub, Cebu, which is the first city in the v3.0 roadmap (Table 5.7). The P30,000 to P40,000 range assumes about 6 to 8 seats across Manila and Cebu at the same rate. Most staff stay remote, so cost grows with partner needs and not with headcount.
