Facility improvements follow the product roadmap in Table 5.7. The move to co-working seats in Year 2 matches the mobile app and Employer Pro release, when we expect partners to ask for onboarding sessions and hiring reviews. The Cebu hub in Year 3 matches regional hub support and the placement dashboard for universities and PESOs. If a milestone slips, we delay the matching facility change.

## **D. Strategy and Plans**

### **D.1 Build, Buy, Partner, or Outsource**

We decided what to build, buy, partner for, or outsource by asking two questions: does it make Hakbang different, and can someone else do it cheaper? We build what makes us different: the Living Profile, the matching engine, the employer dashboard, the verification process, and the brand. These hold our data and our reputation for trust, and a competitor could copy them only by earning that trust. We buy managed services such as Supabase, Vercel, the AI API, and messaging because running our own servers would cost more time and money than a five-student team has. We partner for training content and jobs because employers already own both, and for job seeker access because universities and PESOs already reach graduates. We outsource legal review, accounting, and extra coding because we need them only part of the time.

| Model | What we do this way | Why |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Build in-house | Living Profile, matching engine, employer dashboard, verification process, brand | These form our edge, so we keep control of the code and data |
| Buy (software services) | Supabase, Vercel, LLM API, email, push, and SMS services, analytics | Managed services cost less than building and running our own servers |
| Partner | Training content and jobs from employers; job seeker access from universities and PESOs; introductions from IBPAP later | Partners already own the training and the audiences we need |
| Outsource | Legal review, accounting and tax filing, extra coding if the schedule slips | We need these services only part of the time |

*Table 6.5. Operating Model*

### **D.2 Supplier Dependencies and Backup Plans**

The supplier we depend on most is the partner employer, because without tracks and hiring commitments there is nothing to match. That is why we plan to sign several partners, so no single one holds more than half of our tracks by Year 2\. The technology suppliers come next: Supabase and Vercel hold our data and hosting, but we use standard PostgreSQL and Next.js, so we can move to another host with a monthly export as our safety net. The AI provider and SMS services matter less, because manual entry, email, and web push still work if they fail. University career offices are a referral channel with several substitutes, such as Facebook groups and TikTok content.

| Supplier | What we depend on | Backup |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Partner employers | Training tracks and hiring commitments | Sign several partners so no single one holds more than half of our tracks by Year 2 |
| Supabase | Database, login, file storage | Standard PostgreSQL data that we can move to another host; monthly exports |
| Vercel | Web hosting | Any host that runs Next.js, such as Netlify or a cloud server |
| LLM API provider | Resume reading and skill-gap check | Switch providers or fall back to manual entry |
| SMS and messaging services | Reminders | Email and web push still work |
| University career offices | Job seeker referrals | Graduate Facebook groups, TikTok content, and referral codes |

*Table 6.6. Key Suppliers and Redundancy Plans*

### **D.3 Scaling Without a Matching Rise in Overhead**

Hakbang's costs have to grow slower than its hires. Between Year 1 and Year 3 the plan grows hires six times, from 319 to 1,911, while cost of service stays near 6% of revenue (Table 9.3). Five choices make this possible:

* **Software does the repeat work.** Matching, progress tracking, reminders, and billing reports run in the app. One more trainee adds almost no cost.  
* **Partners supply the training.** We do not hire trainers or build courses as tracks grow.  
* **Automate verification later.** Once the checklist is stable, we will add document upload checks so one operations associate can verify more employers.  
* **Repeat the partner playbook.** The package we use to sign universities and PESOs in Manila (onboarding steps, promotional materials, placement reports) works again in each new city (Ch. II, D.7).  
* **Remote-first team.** We add co-working seats only where partners need face-to-face meetings.

## **E. Regulatory and Legal Issues**

The steps below follow the order the law requires. SEC registration comes first because the BIR and city hall need our corporate registration before they will register us or issue a permit. Tax registration and official receipts follow, then the barangay clearance and business permit. BMBE registration comes after the permit because it is filed with the city treasurer's office and then the BIR. SSS, PhilHealth, and Pag-IBIG registration is needed before the first employee. The DOLE license check and the NPC registration are due before the pilot, because the pilot is when we begin collecting personal data and matching people to jobs. The trademark filing can wait until Year 1 but should not slip, since a conflict could force a rename after the brand is known.

| Requirement | Owner | Agency | When | If we skip it |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Incorporate as a stock corporation; the Revised Corporation Code (RA 11232\) allows 2 to 15 incorporators | CEO, with legal counsel | Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) | Before the pilot invoices | We cannot sign partner agreements or invoice in the company's name |
| Tax registration and official receipts | CFO | Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) | After SEC registration | We cannot issue valid receipts to employers |
| Barangay clearance and business permit | CFO | Barangay and city hall | After SEC registration | We may not operate legally in the city |
| BMBE registration for income tax exemption | CFO | City or municipal treasurer's office, then BIR | After the business permit | We pay income tax we could have been exempt from |
| Employer registration with SSS, PhilHealth, and Pag-IBIG | COO | SSS, PhilHealth, Pag-IBIG Fund | Before the first employee | We cannot hire employees compliantly |
| Confirm whether a recruitment license is needed | COO, with legal counsel | Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) | Before the pilot | We risk penalties or having to stop matching |
| Register the data processing system and data protection officer | COO as Data Protection Officer | National Privacy Commission (NPC) | Before the pilot | We risk NPC penalties and losing the trust of users |
| File the "Hakbang" trademark | CEO, with legal counsel | IPOPHL | Year 1 | A third party could register the name first |

*Table 6.7. Registration and Compliance Steps*

Each step has one named owner, so no filing waits on a group decision. The CFO tracks the dates in a shared checklist and reports progress at the monthly board meeting. Registration fees and permits cost about P15,000 in 2027 (Table 9.3), and the lawyer's fee for the incorporation papers sits in the advisors budget (Table 9.9). If DOLE rules that Hakbang needs a recruitment license, the COO files the application, and the P100,000 reserve from the seed round (Table 10.3) pays the fees and bond.

## **C. Management Compensation and Ownership**

### **C.1 Compensation**

* **Year 1:** No cash pay. Founders work for equity (sweat equity). Paying the Year 2 stipends in 2027 would cost about P1.04 million (Ch. IX, B), and that money stays in the company as cash for Year 2\.  
* **Year 2 (2028):** Monthly stipends start in January 2028, once fees have covered monthly costs for three straight months (the model shows this by September 2027). The CEO receives P20,000 a month, and the COO, CFO, CMO, and CTO receive P15,000 a month each. With 13th month pay and SSS, PhilHealth, and Pag-IBIG, the five stipends cost about P1.17 million in 2028\.  
* **Year 3 (2029):** Stipends become salaries: P40,000 a month for the CEO and P30,000 a month for each of the other four founders, about P2.33 million in total with 13th month pay and contributions (Table 9.3). The CEO earns more because he leads sales and fundraising and carries the largest share of the company’s risk.  
* **Bonuses:** From 2028, a yearly pool of P100 for each hire still employed after 90 days, capped at 10% of income before tax and paid only in profitable years: about P7,700 in 2028 and P132,600 in 2029 (Table 9.3). The board splits the pool among all staff, founders included.  
* **Non-cash incentives:** Equity, startup competition exposure, and leadership experience.

The group may change the split before incorporation.

## **D. Other Investors**

Hakbang has no outside investors yet. The founders fund the Year 1 development and launch costs of about P139,541 (Table 5.8) from their own money, startup competition prizes, and pilot fees. After the pilot, we plan to approach university incubators such as DLSU Animo Labs, angel investors, and government startup programs under the Innovative Startup Act (RA 11337). We plan to raise P2,000,000 for 15% of the company in February 2028, after the Year 1 milestone. Chapter X sets out the terms.

## **E. Employment and Other Agreements and Stock Option and Bonus Plans**

We will put these agreements in writing before incorporation and review them with legal counsel (Table 7.4).

* **Founders’ agreement.** Sets each founder’s role, each founder's share in Table 7.3, 4-year vesting with a 1-year cliff, what happens if a founder leaves, and the transfer of the code, brand, and data to the company.   
* **Employment contracts.** Part-time and full-time hires sign contracts with SSS, PhilHealth, and Pag-IBIG coverage, a confidentiality clause, and an assignment of work created for Hakbang to the company.  
* **Agreements with partners and freelancers.** Partner employers sign the partner agreement in Chapter IV, D.1. Freelance developers sign a non-disclosure agreement and assign their code to Hakbang.  
* **Stock option plan.** A 10% option pool (Table 7.3) for key hires such as the first developers and sales staff. Options vest over 4 years with a 1-year cliff, and the board approves each grant (assumption).  
* **Bonus plan.** A yearly bonus pool tied to hires and 90-day retention, paid only in profitable years (Ch. VII, C.1).

## **F. Board of Directors**

The first board has five seats, one for each founder. Each director has one vote, and the board decides by majority. Board votes are one per director, but shareholder decisions follow the percentages in Table 7.3. It meets once a month to review hires, retention, cash, and major decisions. When outside investors join, we plan to add one independent director with HR technology or IT-BPM experience.

## **G. Other Stakeholders, Rights, and Restrictions**

Hakbang has no outside investors today, and partner employers, universities, and PESOs hold no equity. Founders agree that spending above P100,000 on a single item, taking on debt, or issuing new shares needs board approval (assumption). Future investors may ask for rights such as pro-rata participation, a liquidation preference, or a board observer seat. We will negotiate these with legal counsel when we raise funds.

# **Chapter VIII. Sustainability and Impact**

---

Hakbang's long-term success depends on the same things that make it useful: employers who keep hiring trainees, job seekers who keep trusting the platform, and a team that stays together after graduation.

## **A. Issues of Sustainability of the Venture**

We sorted the threats to Hakbang's survival into internal issues, which the team can control, and external issues, which come from the market or the government. For each one we set a response and a named owner. The most serious threats are partner concentration and a slowdown in IT-BPM hiring, because together they decide how many hires, and therefore how much revenue, Hakbang can earn.

| Issue | Type | Why it threatens the business | Our response | Owner |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Founders leave after graduation | Internal | Five students run every function; losing two would stall sales or development | Four-year vesting (Ch. VII, C.2); stipends from Year 2 and salaries from Year 3; written handover notes for each role | Miguel Borromeo, CEO |
| Depending on a few partner employers | Internal | In Year 1 one or two BPOs supply most tracks; losing one cuts revenue sharply | Sign several partners so none holds more than half of all tracks by Year 2; add retail and logistics employers in Year 3 | Miguel Borromeo, CEO |
| Cash runs short while waiting for payment | Internal | Employers pay 30 days after billing; Year 1 cash falls to about P20,000 in May (Table 9.6) | Monthly cash forecast; seed round after the Year 1 milestone; three-month operating reserve | Francine Santos, CFO |
| Slower IT-BPM hiring or AI replacing entry-level tasks | External | Fewer seats mean fewer hires, and our fee is paid per hire | Add tracks for AI-assisted roles; expand to retail, logistics, and MSME employers (Ch. II, D.6) | Jaztin Jimenez, CMO, with the CEO |
| DOLE requires a recruitment license | External | A license brings fees, a bond, and reporting duties | Ask DOLE before the pilot; if needed, apply using the seed reserve, or partner with a licensed agency | Reinman Ganayo, COO |
| A scam or data breach damages trust | External | Trust is Hakbang's main promise; one incident could stop sign-ups | Strict verification; 48-hour report review; encryption and role-based access; cyber insurance from Year 2 | Hyun Jei Tandingan, Technical Lead, with the COO |
| Large job boards copy train-to-hire | External | Competitors with bigger audiences could add training tracks | Build partner relationships and a record of verified hires that is hard to copy; publish results each quarter | Miguel Borromeo, CEO |

*Table 8.1. Sustainability Issues, Responses, and Owners*

Financially, the plan is built to survive a weaker market. Founders take no cash pay until revenue covers costs, new hires are added only after the hire targets for the previous period are met, and the seed round keeps a reserve for the slow months. Chapter IX, D (Table 9.7) shows that without the seed funding, a year at 60% of planned hires would leave Hakbang short of cash in Year 2, while with it the company stays solvent and has time to cut costs.

## **B. Impact on the Environment**

Hakbang is a digital service, so it has no factory, raw materials, or shipping. Its environmental footprint comes from three sources: the electricity used by cloud servers, the devices the team uses, and the travel of trainees and staff. Of these, travel is the one Hakbang can change most, because train-to-hire programs normally require trainees to report in person for every session.

* **Less commuting for trainees.** Partner tracks can run readings and tests online, so trainees only travel for the sessions that must be face-to-face. If each trainee skips ten round trips across Metro Manila (assumption), the 3,186 hires planned over three years, plus trainees who are not hired, avoid more than 30,000 trips, along with the fuel and fares those trips use.  
* **Paperless onboarding and verification.** Resumes, employer documents, endorsements, and invoices are kept digitally, which removes printed applications and paper files for both job seekers and employers.  
* **Efficient hosting.** We use shared cloud services instead of running our own servers, so we pay for, and use energy for, only the capacity we need.  
* **Longer device life.** The team uses laptops and test phones it already owns and replaces them only when they fail. Retired devices go to accredited e-waste collection points instead of landfill.  
* **Remote-first work.** Most of the team works remotely, and co-working seats are added only where partners need face-to-face meetings (Ch. VI, C.2), which keeps office energy use low.  
* **Weather resilience.** Online modules also let training continue during typhoons and floods, which often close schools and offices in Metro Manila.

## **C. Impact on the Community and Nation**

Hakbang's main contribution is jobs. Every hire it makes is a formal job with a contract and benefits, filled by a graduate who might otherwise have stayed jobless or in work unrelated to their course. This directly supports Sustainable Development Goal 8, Decent Work and Economic Growth.

| Contribution | Year 1 (2027) | Year 2 (2028) | Year 3 (2029) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Formal jobs filled through Hakbang | 319 | 956 | 1,911 |
| Hakbang's own team (founders and staff) | 7 | 10 | 13 |
| Extra income for hires, if each earns P6,000 more a month (assumption) | P23.0 million a year | P68.8 million a year | P137.6 million a year |
| Employer contributions Hakbang pays for its own team (SSS, PhilHealth, Pag-IBIG) | P22,650 | P278,100 | P547,200 |
| Taxes paid or collected by Hakbang | Percentage tax P31,350 | VAT of about P479,642 collected and income tax of P13,926 | VAT of about P1,001,903 and income tax of P238,690 |

*Table 8.2. Projected Social and Economic Contributions*

The income figure assumes that a hire moves from part-time or no work, such as our persona Paolo earning about P12,000 a month in retail, to an entry-level IT-BPM role paying about P18,000 a month. Not every hire will see that full increase, so we treat the figure as an upper estimate. Every hire also gains SSS, PhilHealth, and Pag-IBIG coverage, which informal and part-time work rarely provides.

* **Protection from job scams.** Verified employers, a ban on trainee fees, and the report button give graduates a safer place to look for work. Our social media content also teaches job seekers how to spot fake postings.  
* **Support for schools and local governments.** Universities and PESOs receive aggregate placement reports that help them track graduate employment and plan programs, at no cost to them.  
* **Free career workshops.** We co-host resume and interview workshops with partner career offices, open to all graduating students and not only Hakbang users.  
* **Jobs outside Metro Manila.** From Year 3 the Cebu hub, followed by Davao, Iloilo, and Bacolod, brings the same train-to-hire model to regional graduates, so they can find work without moving to the capital.  
* **Lower hiring costs for employers.** Employers spend less training money on people who quit, which helps IT-BPM firms stay competitive and keep jobs in the country.

## **E. Break-Even Chart and Calculation**

Hakbang earns most of its money per hire, so we measure break-even in hires. Each hire brings in its average fee less the 5% guarantee credit, the P150 variable cost, and bank fees. That amount is the contribution margin. Fixed costs are everything else, less the Employer Pro and featured listing income, which does not depend on hires.

Break-even hires \= (fixed costs − subscription and listing income) ÷ contribution margin per hire

| Item | Year 1 (2027) | Year 2 (2028) | Year 3 (2029) |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Average fee per hire | 4,561 | 4,250 | 4,275 |
| Contribution margin per hire | 4,311 | 3,867 | 3,891 |
| Fixed costs for the year | 592,041 | 3,909,100 | 7,116,600 |
| Less: subscription and listing income | 0 | 290,000 | 1,010,000 |
| **Break-even hires per year** | **137** | **936** | **1,569** |
| Break-even hires per month | about 11 | about 78 | about 131 |
| Planned hires | 319 | 956 | 1,911 |
| Margin of safety | 57% | 2% | 18% |

*Table 9.8. Break-Even Calculation*

![][image18]

*Figure 9.1. Year 2 Break-Even Chart*

Year 2 is the risky year: Hakbang needs 936 of its 956 planned hires to break even, a margin of only 2%. The CFO will track hires against the 78-a-month line every month. If two months in a row fall below it, the CEO delays the July 2028 hires (content and support associates) until the line is met again. In Year 1, monthly fees pass monthly costs in July 2027, the third month of hiring.

## **F. Cost Control**

Most of Hakbang's spending is people. Payroll takes 33% of total costs in Year 1, 61% in Year 2, and 66% in Year 3, so hiring decisions control the budget. The team set these rules:

* **Hire on proof.** Each planned hire waits until the hire target for the period before it is met (Table 7.1). The board approves every new salary.  
* **Spending limits.** The CFO approves any expense above P10,000. The board approves any single item above P100,000, any loan, and any new shares (Ch. VII, G).  
* **Cloud and AI caps.** The CTO sets usage alerts on Supabase and Vercel and a monthly spending cap on the AI API (Table 5.5).  
* **Pay-per-result marketing.** Micro-influencers earn per sign-up, and we stop any channel whose cost per sign-up exceeds P100 (assumption).  
* **Monthly review.** The CFO compares actual results with this model at each monthly board meeting: hires, cost per hire, cash, and days to collect.

Professional advisors are the second-largest cost after payroll in Year 1\. We hire them per task or on small retainers instead of hiring staff, because Hakbang needs legal, accounting, and audit work only a few times a year. Table 9.9 shows the budget. The legal review of the privacy policy, terms, and partner agreement (P20,000) sits in Table 5.8 and is not repeated here.

## **G. Highlights**

* **Revenue** grows from P1.38 million in 2027 to P4.15 million in 2028 and P8.77 million in 2029\.  
* **Gross margin** stays above 93% in all three years, since partners supply the training.  
* **Net income** is P834,984 in 2027 (with unpaid founders), P55,703 in 2028, and P954,758 in 2029\.  
* **Break-even** comes at 137 hires in 2027, 936 in 2028, and 1,569 in 2029\.  
* **Lowest cash** is about P20,000 in May 2027, before the first collections.  
* **Funding** is P180,000 from the founders and a P2,000,000 seed round in February 2028 (Ch. X). At 60% of planned hires, the seed round keeps the company solvent through 2028, and the cost cuts in Table 9.7 keep it solvent through 2029\.  
* **Cash at the end of 2029** is about P3.3 million, with no debt.

# **Chapter X. Proposed Company Offering**

# ---

## **A. Desired Financing**

Hakbang seeks P2,000,000 in seed funding, to close in February 2028\. We raise after the December 2027 go/no-go review (Table 5.3), when the board can show investors at least three active employer partners, about 319 hires, and the 90-day retention results from the pilot. Raising after these results, and not before the pilot, lets the founders sell a smaller share of the company.

The amount comes from the cash flow model in Chapter IX. The founders' P180,000 and the Year 1 fees cover the pilot and launch. The seed round pays for Year 2, when payroll rises to about P208,000 a month and Hakbang builds the mobile app, and it keeps a three-month reserve in the bank. Table 9.7 shows why the reserve matters: at 60% of planned hires, the company would run out of cash in February 2028 without it. We will accept a minimum of P1,500,000. If we raise only the minimum, we cut the reserve to two months and delay the July 2028 hires.

| ----- | ----- |
| Amount | P2,000,000 (minimum P1,500,000) |
| Security | Common shares of the company |
| Equity offered | 15% of the company after the round |
| Valuation | P11.33 million before the round; P13.33 million after |
| Price per share | About P56.67 (35,294 new shares) |
| Target investors | Angel investors, university incubators such as DLSU Animo Labs, and startup grant programs under the Innovative Startup Act (RA 11337); grants reduce the equity we sell |
| Investor rights | Quarterly financial reports; right to join future rounds to keep their share (pro-rata); one board observer seat for the lead investor |
| Restrictions | Founders' shares stay under the 4-year vesting in Table 7.3; no founder may sell shares for 3 years without board approval |
| Target close | February 2028 |

*Table 10.1. Summary of the Proposed Offering*

We chose common shares over a loan because Hakbang's cash comes in uneven batches as training tracks finish, and a loan needs fixed monthly payments. We chose a priced round over a convertible note because Philippine angels and incubators know the share structure under the Revised Corporation Code, and the founders already hold common shares with vesting. The P11.33 million pre-money value is about 2.7 times our Year 2 revenue forecast (assumption). Legal counsel will draft the subscription agreement, using the P60,000 set aside in Table 9.9.

## **C. Capitalization**

| Shareholder | Shares before the round | Ownership before | Shares after the round | Ownership after |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Miguel Borromeo, CEO | 48,000 | 24.0% | 48,000 | 20.4% |
| Reinman Ganayo, COO | 33,000 | 16.5% | 33,000 | 14.0% |
| Francine Santos, CFO | 33,000 | 16.5% | 33,000 | 14.0% |
| Jaztin Jimenez, CMO | 33,000 | 16.5% | 33,000 | 14.0% |
| Hyun Jei Tandingan, CTO | 33,000 | 16.5% | 33,000 | 14.0% |
| Employee option pool | 20,000 | 10.0% | 20,000 | 8.5% |
| Seed investors | 0 | 0.0% | 35,294 | 15.0% |
| **Total** | **200,000** | **100.0%** | **235,294** | **100.0%** |

*Table 10.2. Capitalization Before and After the Seed Round*

After the round the founders still hold 76.5% of the company, and the CEO remains the largest shareholder. Paid-in capital rises from P180,000 to P2,180,000 (Table 9.4). Hakbang has no debt before or after the round.

## **D. Use of Funds**

| Use | Amount (P) | Share | What it pays for |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Operating reserve | 1,000,000 | 50% | About three months of Year 2 cash costs, kept in the bank for slow months and late payers |
| Product v2.0 | 308,000 | 15% | Android and iOS apps, machine learning matching, Employer Pro dashboard, evening and weekend tracks (Table 5.7) |
| Year 2 hires ahead of revenue | 262,000 | 13% | First months of pay for the B2B sales, content, and support associates before their work brings in fees |
| Marketing | 150,000 | 8% | \#UnangHakbang 2028 campaign and outreach to underemployed young workers (Segment B) |
| Equipment | 120,000 | 6% | Three laptops for new hires |
| DOLE license reserve | 100,000 | 5% | Fees and bond if DOLE rules that Hakbang needs a recruitment license (Table 5.6) |
| Legal costs of the round | 60,000 | 3% | Subscription agreement, amended articles, and SEC filings |
| **Total** | **2,000,000** | **100%** |  |

*Table 10.3. Use of Seed Funds*

The CFO reports spending against Table 10.3 to the board each month and to investors each quarter. If DOLE does not require a license, the P100,000 reserve moves to marketing.

## **E. Investor's Return**

Seed investors earn their return when they sell their shares, either to a larger HR technology company that buys Hakbang or to a later investor in a Series A round. We do not plan to pay dividends before 2031, because profits go back into growth. To estimate the return, we extend the plan two more years: hires grow about 50% in 2030 and 40% in 2031 as the Cebu, Davao, Iloilo, and Bacolod hubs open, which puts 2031 revenue at about P18 million (assumption). We also assume a Series A round in 2030 cuts the seed investors' 15% to about 12%.

| Exit value in 2031 | Multiple of 2031 revenue | Value of the investors' 12% | Return on P2,000,000 | Yearly return (about 4 years) |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| P27 million | 1.5x | P3.24 million | 1.6 times | 13% |
| P36 million | 2.0x | P4.32 million | 2.2 times | 21% |
| P54 million | 3.0x | P6.48 million | 3.2 times | 34% |

*Table 10.4. Estimated Return to Seed Investors (assumption)*

In the middle case, an investor who puts in P2,000,000 in 2028 holds shares worth about P4.3 million in 2031\. The return depends on two things the investor can track every quarter: whether Hakbang keeps its hire targets, and whether partners stay past their first 12-month agreement. If Hakbang misses its targets, the operating reserve and the cost cuts in Table 9.7 protect the investors' money while the board changes course.

# **Exhibit**

## **A. User Flow**

Figure E.1 shows how the three users of Hakbang move through the platform during the pilot. The job seeker signs up, builds a Living Profile, applies to a matched track, trains, and confirms the job contract. The employer gets verified, posts a track, accepts trainees, marks hires, and pays only for confirmed hires. The Hakbang admin checks each employer's documents before any track goes live and reviews every report within 48 hours. The flow follows the eight-step script in our MVP demo.
